title: Subexponential-time Circuit-SAT
formal:
Does there exist one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\), an integer \(d\ge1\), a constant \(K\ge1\), and a function \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with \(\lim_{n\to\infty}g(n)/n=0\), such that \(A\) decides satisfiability of every explicitly given Boolean circuit with \(n\ge1\) input variables and \(s\ge0\) gates in at most
\[
K\,2^{g(n)}(L+1)^d
\]
Turing-machine bit steps? Here \(L\) is the full binary encoding length, gates are binary AND and OR and unary NOT, and depth and fan-out are unrestricted. The output must be correct on every circuit. The requested bound is abbreviated \(2^{o(n)}\operatorname{poly}(L)\); its exponential parameter is the number of input variables, not the number of gates or encoding bits.
definitions:
A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose nodes are the constants 0 and 1, input variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), and operation gates, together with one designated output node. AND and OR have two incoming arguments and NOT has one. Gate values may be reused by any number of later gates. Size \(s\) counts operation gates only. The output may be a gate, an input or a constant. No bound on depth, sharing or gate count as a function of \(n\) is imposed; in particular, the target includes every polynomial circuit size with the same polynomial overhead exponent \(d\).

For an assignment \(a\in\{0,1\}^n\), evaluate gates in topological order using ordinary Boolean operations. Satisfiability means that at least one such assignment gives output 1. The algorithm returns exactly this yes/no answer; it need not count or enumerate satisfying assignments. All declared input nodes are explicitly listed and included in \(n\), even if some are unused.

Fix the following binary encoding. Encode an integer \(z\ge0\) by \(1^b0\) followed by the \(b\)-bit binary expansion of \(z+1\), where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(z+1)\rfloor+1\). List the codes of \(n,s\), then \(n\) input-node markers, and then the \(s\) gates in a topological order. Number the constants 0 and 1 first, the inputs next and the gates last. Each gate has a two-bit type tag and coded predecessor indices, all smaller than its own index. Finish with the coded output-node index, with no trailing data. Invalid encodings are outside the domain. The total length \(L\) is \(O((n+s)\log(n+s+2))\); the polynomial factor pays for processing the entire explicit description.

The algorithm is one classical deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no advice, no oracle and no random bits. All input processing, intermediate bit computation and output are charged. The constants, function and program are chosen before the input: the quantifier order is \(\exists(A,d,K,g)\;\forall C\), subject to the displayed limit on \(g\). In particular, \(g\) depends only on \(n\), and \(d\) cannot grow with circuit size or an accuracy parameter. The limit means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there is an integer \(N\) such that \(g(n)\le\varepsilon n\) for every \(n\ge N\). Thus one fixed saving \(2^{(1-\delta)n}\) for a constant \(0<\delta<1\) does not by itself meet this target.

context_blocks.text: Circuit satisfiability asks whether a Boolean computation accepts any assignment to its inputs. The 2013 Dagstuhl report distinguishes its exponential-time behavior from that of formulas whose clauses have bounded width, despite their polynomial-time equivalence.

Williams proves conditional connections between satisfiability running times at different circuit sizes, including consequences giving subexponential algorithms for smaller circuits. These are implications from algorithmic assumptions, not an unconditional algorithm meeting this card.

This target implies the positive answer to TCS-7270, which asks only for a fixed exponential saving at each fixed linear gate density. The converse is not asserted: the present question requires a vanishing exponential rate and covers general gate counts.

An October 2026 OpenAI preprint claims subexponential counting for each fixed clause width. That theorem is stated for formulas in conjunctive normal form, meaning conjunctions of clauses that are disjunctions of literals (variables or their negations). It is not stated for general circuits measured by their original input variables. Introducing a variable for each gate can increase the variable count to \(n+s\), so that conversion alone does not establish the bound requested here. The preprint is recorded as a claim; its proof and formalization were not independently audited in this addition.

why: Determining whether general circuit satisfiability admits a vanishing exponential rate would identify a fundamental boundary of exact algorithms, beyond fixed improvements to exhaustive search or restrictions to simple circuit families.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must supply a single deterministic algorithm, prove exact decision correctness on every encoded circuit, and prove the full charged running-time bound with fixed \(d,K\) and \(g(n)/n\to0\). A negative answer must unconditionally rule out every such algorithm and bound; a lower bound conditional on another conjecture establishes only that conditional statement.

An algorithm restricted to linear-size circuits, bounded depth, formulas or a fixed clause width does not establish this universal target. A running time subexponential only in \(L\) or \(n+s\), or a fixed positive saving in the coefficient of \(n\), also does not suffice. This is a genuine existence question, not a numerical request to approximate an infimum running-time exponent.

sentences: The input is an explicitly listed Boolean circuit with no depth or sharing restriction.
The task is to decide exactly whether some assignment to its input variables makes the output true.
One deterministic algorithm must run in \(2^{o(n)}\operatorname{poly}(L)\) time, where \(n\) counts input variables and \(L\) is the full encoding length.
The polynomial overhead is fixed for all circuit sizes, so a result only for linear-size circuits or fixed-width formulas does not establish the target.
A complete Lean-checked proof of the existence claim or its unconditional negation is required.
